title: Remove a Key From a Search Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree with distinct values (every value in a left subtree is smaller than its ancestor, every value in a right subtree is larger) and a number key.

Remove the node holding key and return the root of the resulting tree, which must still be a valid binary search tree containing every other value. If key is not in the tree, return it unchanged.

Several shapes are valid after a removal; any valid search tree with the right values is accepted. Aim for O(h) time, where h is the tree height.

examples.why: 3 has two children. Its in-order successor, 6 (the smallest value in its right subtree), takes its place. Promoting 1 instead would also be valid.
A leaf is simply cut off.
7 is not in the tree, so nothing changes.

hints: First find the node: go left or right by comparing with key, as in any search tree lookup. Then think about how many children it has.
No children: remove it. One child: let the child take its place. The hard case is two children.

With two children, copy in the smallest value of the right subtree (the in-order successor), then remove that value from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that second removal is an easy case.

explain.intuition:
Finding the node is a normal search-tree walk. Removing it is easy unless it has two children, because then two subtrees need one parent. The trick is to find a value that can sit in its spot without breaking the order: the in-order successor, the smallest value in the right subtree. It is bigger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right.

Copy the successor's value into the node, then remove the successor from the right subtree. The successor is the leftmost node there, so it has no left child, and removing it is one of the easy cases. Everything happens along one root-to-leaf path, so the time is O(h).
steps: If the node is empty, return it (key not found).
If key is smaller, recurse left and store the result as the new left child; if larger, do the same on the right.
If this node holds key and has at most one child, return that child (or null).
Otherwise find the leftmost node of the right subtree, copy its value here, and remove that value from the right subtree.
pitfalls: Forgetting to reattach the result of the recursive call (node.left = remove(node.left, key)). The parent then still points at the removed node.
Picking the successor from the wrong subtree, or the largest value of the right subtree, which breaks the ordering.
Returning the original root when the root itself is removed. The new root may be a child or a different node.

solutions.title: Hang the left subtree under the successor
solutions.idea: When the node has two children, attach its whole left subtree as the left child of the leftmost node in its right subtree, and return the right subtree. Valid, but it can make the tree taller.

solutions.title: Replace with the in-order successor
solutions.idea: Recursive removal. With two children, copy the smallest value of the right subtree into the node and remove that value from the right subtree.

followups: Node values are large objects you must not copy. Relink the successor node itself instead of copying its value.
Keep the tree balanced after removals. What does a self-balancing tree (AVL, red-black) add on the way back up?
